markscheme_points.text: angle (subtended at centre of a circle) when arc (length) = radius

hints: Hint 1: Think about what an angle in radians compares - look at the curved edge of a circle and its distance from the centre.
parts.proper_answer: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc of length equal to the radius.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture What a Radian Measures**
Think of cutting a piece of the circumference exactly as long as the radius and looking at the angle it makes at the centre. That special angle is 1 radian. So a definition must link angle, arc length and radius together.

Step 2: **Give the Exact Definition**
$$ \text{1 rad is the angle when arc length = radius} $$ That is all that is needed for the mark.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
The rear wheel and the pedals of a bicycle are connected by a chain that passes around two cogs (toothed wheels), as shown in Fig. 1.1.

{{figure:figure_1_1}}

Fig. 1.1 (not to scale)

The small cog has a radius of $0.038\text{ m}$ and is fixed to the rear wheel so that it rotates with it. The large cog has a radius of $0.15\text{ m}$ and is fixed to the pedals so that it rotates with them. The rear wheel has a radius of $0.46\text{ m}$.

The bicycle is being pedalled so that it moves in a straight line at a constant speed of $17\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
parts.text: Calculate the angular speed of the rear wheel.
hints: Hint 1: The edge of the rear wheel touching the ground moves forward at the same linear speed as the bicycle, 17 m s-1. Which radius links this to rotation?
Hint 2: Recall how linear speed $v$ and angular speed $\omega$ are linked for a point at radius $r$, then rearrange for $\omega$ before substituting.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Forward Speed to Spinning**
For rolling without slipping, the centre moves forward at $v = 17 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the rim rotates so that $v = r\omega$. Here use the rear wheel radius $r = 0.46 \text{ m}$, not the cog radius.

Step 2: **Calculate Angular Speed**
$$ \omega = \frac{v}{r} $$ $$ \omega = \frac{17}{0.46} = 37 \text{ rad s}^{-1} $$ to 2 s.f. Units are $\text{rad s}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the period of rotation of the small cog.
hints: Hint 1: The small cog is fixed to the rear wheel, so what does that tell you about its angular speed and period compared to the wheel?
Hint 2: Think how long one full $2\pi$ rad rotation takes if you know the rate in rad per second.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Same Rotation Rate**
The small cog is fixed to the rear wheel so it rotates with it. It has the same $\omega = 37 \text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and same period $T$. One rotation is an angle of $2\pi$ rad.

Step 2: **Calculate the Period**
$$ T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi r}{v} $$ $$ T = \frac{2\pi}{37} = \frac{2\pi \times 0.46}{17} = 0.17 \text{ s} $$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Show that the distance moved by point X on the chain during one full rotation of the small cog is $0.24\text{ m}$.
hints: Hint 1: Point X is on the chain wrapped round the small cog, so in one turn the chain must move by the outer edge length of that cog.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Show the Chain Distance**
In one full rotation the cog pulls a length of chain equal to its circumference:
$$ \text{distance} = 2\pi r $$ $$ \text{distance} = 2\pi \times 0.038 = 0.239 \text{ m} \approx 0.24 \text{ m} $$ This is the distance moved by point X.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Use the information in (b)(iii) to determine the angle through which the large cog rotates during one full rotation of the small cog.
hints: Hint 1: The same length of chain, 0.24 m, must move round the edge of the large cog. Is this length an arc length for that cog?
Hint 2: Recall how arc length $s$, radius $r$ and angle $\theta$ in radians are related, then use the large cog radius 0.15 m.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Angle = Arc / Radius**
The chain does not stretch, so the large cog also has $s = 0.24 \text{ m}$ of its rim pass by. For any circle:
$$ \theta = \frac{s}{r} $$

Step 2: **Calculate for the Large Cog**
$$ \theta = \frac{0.24}{0.15} = 1.6 \text{ rad} $$ Note this is much less than $2\pi$ rad, as expected because the large cog is bigger and turns more slowly.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The chain of the bicycle in (b) is moved onto a smaller cog fixed to the rear wheel. The speed of the bicycle does not change.

Explain, without calculation, the effect of this change on the angular speed of the pedals.

markscheme_points.text: point X moves through a smaller distance in the same time or (linear) speed of movement of point X / chain decreases or (linear) speed of (circumference of) both cogs decreases

hints: Hint 1: Bicycle speed is unchanged, so the rear wheel angular speed is unchanged. If the rear cog is now smaller but spinning at the same rate, what happens to the linear speed of its rim and hence the chain?
Hint 2: That chain speed is also the rim speed of the large front cog, whose radius has not changed. What must happen to its angular speed to give a lower rim speed?
parts.proper_answer: With the same bicycle speed the rear wheel and small cog rotate at the same angular speed, but the smaller radius gives a smaller linear speed of the rim and chain. The large cog rim moves at this reduced chain speed, so with unchanged radius its angular speed, and hence pedal angular speed, decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Follow the Chain Speed**
Bicycle speed is the same, so $\omega$ of the rear wheel is the same. Linear rim speed is $v = r\omega$. With a smaller rear cog radius $r$, $v$ of the cog rim is smaller, so the chain speed and distance moved per second by point X decreases.

Step 2: **Link to the Pedals**
The large cog is driven by the chain, so its rim linear speed also decreases. Since its radius is unchanged and $\omega = v/r$, its angular speed must decrease. The pedals are fixed to the large cog, so the angular speed of the pedals decreases.
